messages.content: You write the short explanations that first-year programming students in India type when a C quiz asks them "Why did you choose that answer?". Reply with a JSON object only.

A student was shown this C code and question.

Code:
char x[] = "ok";
char y[] = "ok";
int same = (x == y);

Question: What is same?
The student answered: 1

The student holds this wrong belief and does not know it is wrong: `==` compares text

Write 5 different explanations this student might type for why they chose that answer.
Voice: long-winded, walks through the steps one by one, 20 to 35 words.

Rules:
- Each one must show the student's reasoning, not just repeat the answer.
- Write as the student, in the first person or with no subject. Do not judge the answer or say it is wrong.
- Do not name the idea as a rule and do not use textbook terms for the mistake.
- Make the 5 explanations differ in wording and in which part of the code they point at.

Return JSON: {"sentences": ["...", "..."]}

content: {"sentences": ["So x is \"ok\" and y is also \"ok\", so when I check if they're the same with ==, the text matches exactly, giving 1.", "Looking at the two char arrays, both contain the letters o and k, so comparing them with == should mean comparing the actual characters.", "The == operator checks if the left side equals the right side, and since both say \"ok\", they equal each other, so same becomes true.", "First x gets \"ok\", then y gets \"ok\", so both variables hold identical strings; == then tells me they are the same, which is 1.", "Both arrays end up with the same text inside, so when I put x == y, it looks at the text and sees they match, returning 1."]}

sentences: So x is "ok" and y is also "ok", so when I check if they're the same with ==, the text matches exactly, giving 1.
Looking at the two char arrays, both contain the letters o and k, so comparing them with == should mean comparing the actual characters.
The == operator checks if the left side equals the right side, and since both say "ok", they equal each other, so same becomes true.
First x gets "ok", then y gets "ok", so both variables hold identical strings; == then tells me they are the same, which is 1.
Both arrays end up with the same text inside, so when I put x == y, it looks at the text and sees they match, returning 1.
